gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 140 W these banks advertise only arrives as 28 V × 5 A over USB PD 3.1 EPR, which needs an EPR (240 W) cable and a laptop that accepts EPR on that port. A 3 A cable stops at 60 W and a 100 W (20 V/5 A) cable stops at 100 W. Apple says a 16-inch MacBook Pro fast-charges from a USB-C source only through a USB-C-to-MagSafe 3 cable, or, on the Nov 2023 or later models, through its 240 W USB-C cable.
standout_why: I opened Popular Science (cited), Expert Reviews (cited), Wirecutter via the proxy (cited) and Android Central (cited). Wired's page would not fetch. Popular Science says only that a 100 W cable is needed for laptops and does not mention EPR, 28 V or a 240 W cable. Expert Reviews says PD 3.1 banks 'don't go over 28V at 5A for a maximum of 140W' and work 'with compatible devices and cables' but never names the cable or the laptop requirement. Wirecutter gives the rating of each included cable: Anker Prime 240 W, UGREEN 145W 140 W. It does not say that other cables, or MacBook Pro 16 USB-C ports, cap the output. Android Central's page came back truncated with no relevant text. None of them has Apple's MagSafe 3 / Nov 2023 240 W cable rule or the 60 W / 100 W cable caps. Wirecutter's cable ratings cover only part of the finding, so this is 2, not 3.
decides: This confirms the 140 W tier (Anker Prime 26K, UGREEN 145W/200W, AOHi Starship 240W) only for a shopper with a 16-inch MacBook Pro or another EPR laptop who also uses an EPR cable. For a 16-inch MacBook Pro, the page should say to charge it through Apple's USB-C-to-MagSafe 3 cable or, on Nov 2023 or later models, through a 240 W USB-C cable. ChargerLab measured 133.47 W from the AOHi into an M4 Pro MacBook Pro over MagSafe 3. On any other cable, or on a 13–14-inch laptop or a MacBook Air, the bank tops out at 100 W or less. That makes the cheaper 100 W class (for example the UGREEN 130W at $67.99) the right pick for those buyers. One trap to flag: UGREEN sells its 145W bank in a bundle with 100 W cables, and those cables cannot carry 140 W.

findings.label: Cable and mode needed for each USB PD power level
findings.value: 3 A profiles (5–20 V) cover 15–60 W. 20 V/5 A (>60–100 W) 'Requires 5A cable'. 28/36/48 V at 5 A (>100–240 W) 'Requires entry into EPR mode' and 'Requires EPR cable'.
findings.source_title: SSZTD49 Technical article | TI.com (Table 1, SPR and EPR fixed voltage ranges)
findings.note: Texas Instruments' summary of the USB PD 3.1 table. The 140 W banks reach 140 W only at the 28 V × 5 A EPR level, so a 100 W (20 V/5 A) cable caps them at 100 W and a 3 A cable at 60 W. I did not open the USB-IF spec itself.

findings.label: Apple's rule for fast-charging a 16-inch MacBook Pro
findings.value: 140W USB-C Power Adapter with a USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable, or the 140W adapter with the 240W USB-C Charge Cable, which applies only to the MacBook Pro (16-inch, Nov 2023) or later. Fast charge is about 50% in about 30 minutes.
findings.source_title: Fast charge your MacBook Air or MacBook Pro – Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's listing for 14-inch MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs accepts 96 W or 70 W adapters with either cable, so those laptops gain nothing from a 140 W port. A power bank can stand in for the 140 W adapter only if it offers 28 V EPR.

findings.label: Why the 2021 16-inch MacBook Pro's USB-C ports did not take 140 W
findings.value: Full 140 W needed 'Apple's proprietary USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable' because 'there are no USB-C to USB-C cables currently available that support 240 W EPR'. The article says that without EPR, USB-C allows only up to 100 W.
findings.source_title: Apple 16-inch MacBook Pro becomes the first device to support USB-C Extended Power Range but 140 W fast charging is limited to MagSafe 3 for now – Notebookcheck (Vaidyanathan Subramaniam, 2021-10-20)
findings.note: This agrees with Apple's current page, where the 240 W USB-C cable route applies only to Nov 2023 or later models.

findings.label: ChargerLab measured 140 W-class output into a MacBook Pro
findings.value: 27.77 V × 4.81 A = 133.47 W into a MacBook Pro M4 Pro through USB-C1 with Apple's MagSafe 3 cable. Both ports together: 118.68 W + 94.17 W. In a sustained 28 V/5 A discharge, temperature protection stopped the test after 10 minutes, with about 24.06 Wh delivered.
findings.source_title: Review of AOHi Starship 240W PD3.1 27600mAh Power Bank (AOC-P011) – ChargerLab (2025-04-28)
findings.note: ChargerLab got the 28 V level through MagSafe 3, which is Apple's supported route. ChargerLab lists the 28V5A profile as 'USB-C1 Output … 28V5A 140W Max' and also reports AVS at 15–28 V. The included cable is engraved '140W'.
